report_title: Ballistic Bobcat (Sponsor / "Sponsoring Access" campaign; overlaps APT35 / Charming Kitten / Phosphorus) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: ESET Research 'Sponsor batch-filed whiskers: Ballistic Bobcat's Scan & Strike backdoor' (2023-09-11, https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/sponsor-batch-filed-whiskers-ballistic-bobcats-scan-strike-backdoor/); ESET malware-ioc repository (https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc); MITRE ATT&CK Group Charming Kitten G0058 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0058/, cited for cluster overlap only)

actor.name: Ballistic Bobcat
actor.mitre_canonical_name: Charming Kitten (overlapping cluster; ESET tracks the Ballistic Bobcat activity group distinctly)
related_clusters: APT35 / Charming Kitten / Phosphorus (activity overlaps; ESET treats Ballistic Bobcat as its own cluster while noting the overlap)
PowerLess backdoor operators (prior Ballistic Bobcat toolset; C2 162.55.137.20 overlaps into the Sponsor timeframe)

Overlaps Charming Kitten / APT35 / Phosphorus / Mint Sandstorm / TA453 / Newscaster (MITRE G0059) - ESET tracks Ballistic Bobcat as a distinct activity group within that overlap; those names identify Charming Kitten (the separate charming-kitten pack), not this cluster.
actor.attribution: Iran-aligned activity group. ESET tracks Ballistic Bobcat as a distinct cluster whose activity overlaps with the group publicly reported as APT35 / Charming Kitten / Phosphorus / Mint Sandstorm. The overlap is acknowledged honestly rather than collapsed into a single identity — infrastructure, victimology (Israel-heavy), and the Sponsor backdoor are the ESET-tracked basis. This is opportunistic 'scan-and-exploit' targeting of already-vulnerable, in some cases already-known-victim, internet-facing hosts rather than deliberate spearphishing of specific organizations.

key_campaigns.name: Sponsoring Access (Sponsor backdoor campaign)
key_campaigns.date: September 2021 to April 2022 (Sponsor deployments; related tooling from mid-2021)
key_campaigns.summary: Ballistic Bobcat compromised at least 34 organizations — ~31 in Israel plus one each in Brazil and the UAE — via scan-and-exploit of internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers (ProxyLogon/ProxyShell-era, CVE-2021-26855). On vulnerable hosts the actor dropped batch-file installers that write config files to disk (config.txt, node.txt, error.txt) and register the Sponsor backdoor as a Windows service (SystemNetwork in v1; Update in v2-v5). Sponsor collects host reconnaissance, beacons over HTTP/80 with Base64-encoded, RC4-encrypted messages, and executes operator commands (shell exec, download-and-execute). The actor deployed a suite of open-source and dual-use tools (Mimikatz, ProcDump, WebBrowserPassView, Host2IP, SharpTShipper, Plink, RevSocks, GOST, Chisel, SQLExtractor) for credential access, discovery, and tunneling.

malware: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
PowerLess (prior Ballistic Bobcat backdoor; infrastructure overlap)

ttps.procedure_description: Ballistic Bobcat conducts 'scan-and-exploit' behavior — mass scanning the internet for hosts with unpatched, exploitable vulnerabilities (notably Microsoft Exchange) and treating any vulnerable host as an opportunity rather than pursuing pre-selected targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim internet-wide scanning is not endpoint-observable; inbound probes may register at the perimeter but attribution to this actor is weak; hunt/intel candidate via external attack-surface monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: The actor develops and iterates its own Sponsor backdoor across at least five versions (v1-v5, the last aka Alumina), evolving configuration handling, service naming, and evasion between builds.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — malware development occurs off-victim; the resulting binaries are where detection lands; intel/hunt candidate via sample tracking and YARA over the Sponsor family

ttps.procedure_description: The actor obtains and operationalizes publicly available offensive and dual-use tools: Mimikatz, ProcDump, WebBrowserPassView, Host2IP, SharpTShipper, SQLExtractor, Plink, RevSocks, GOST, and Chisel.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition itself is off-endpoint; downstream execution of each tool is the detection surface; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Primary initial-access vector: exploitation of internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers (ProxyLogon/ProxyShell-era, CVE-2021-26855) on already-vulnerable, sometimes already-known-victim hosts, to gain a foothold before dropping the Sponsor backdoor.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — exploitation of CVE-2021-26855 on Exchange is a strong detection surface: IIS/Exchange request logs, W3SVC anomalies, unexpected child processes of w3wp.exe/UMWorkerProcess, webshell writes to Exchange web roots, and version/patch-state monitoring all apply

ttps.procedure_description: Following Exchange exploitation the actor stages files under the Exchange/IIS web root and related paths (e.g. %SYSTEMDRIVE%\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\, %WINDIR%\INF\MSExchange Delivery DSN\) consistent with webshell-mediated access on the compromised server prior to backdoor installation.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — file-integrity monitoring on Exchange/IIS web roots (inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client) and anomalous file writes by w3wp.exe are high-fidelity, actor-relevant detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Installation and operation are driven by batch scripts (install.bat, Uninstall.bat) executed via cmd.exe; the Sponsor backdoor's 'e' operator command runs arbitrary shell commands with cmd.exe /c.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe spawning from a service process or from batch installers, and cmd.exe /c children of the Sponsor service binary, are directly observable via process-creation telemetry (Event ID 4688 / Sysmon 1)

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor requires the 'install' runtime argument to execute its installation routine, invoked by the actor's batch-file installer rather than the victim; captured here as the controlled-argument launch behavior of the dropper chain.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the specific 'install' command-line argument on the Sponsor binary is a detectable string in process-creation logs, but requires knowing the binary name/argument pattern

ttps.technique_name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
ttps.procedure_description: The batch installer registers the Sponsor backdoor as a Windows service configured for automatic startup with full access — named 'SystemNetwork' in v1 and 'Update' in v2 through v5 — providing boot-persistent execution.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — service creation (Event ID 7045 / 4697) with the names SystemNetwork or Update pointing at an unsigned binary in an unusual path is a high-fidelity, actor-specific detection

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor runs as a registered Windows service; execution of the payload is achieved through the Service Control Manager starting the SystemNetwork/Update service.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — services.exe launching an unsigned backdoor binary from a non-standard path is observable via service-start and process-lineage telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Sponsor reads configuration and C2 parameters from on-disk config files (config.txt, node.txt, error.txt) and decodes/decrypts its command-and-control messages (Base64 + RC4) at runtime.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the on-disk config files (config.txt, node.txt, error.txt) co-located with the service binary are a detectable file-artifact pattern, though the decode logic itself is in-memory

ttps.procedure_description: Sponsor stores its operational parameters in obfuscated on-disk configuration files and obfuscates its network traffic; ESET notes evasion improvements across backdoor versions.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — high-entropy config files adjacent to a service binary are detectable via file-entropy analytics, but need dedicated scanning

ttps.technique_name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
ttps.procedure_description: The actor names its service 'SystemNetwork'/'Update' and drops the RevSocks reverse-proxy tool as CSRSS.EXE to masquerade as the legitimate Windows Client/Server Runtime Subsystem; tooling is staged in Windows-legitimate paths such as %WINDIR%\Tasks\ and %WINDIR%\INF\.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — a CSRSS.EXE running from a path other than %WINDIR%\System32 (or with a non-Microsoft signature) is a rare, high-fidelity masquerade detection via image-path/signature analytics

ttps.procedure_description: The actor leverages valid local accounts on compromised hosts (following credential theft) to execute tooling with elevated privileges and to blend backdoor operations with legitimate activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — reuse of local credentials is detectable via anomalous local-logon analytics but blends with legitimate administration

ttps.procedure_description: The actor deploys ProcDump (procdump64.exe) to dump LSASS process memory and Mimikatz (mi.exe) to extract credentials from that memory / the local system.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — procdump against lsass.exe (command line containing lsass / -ma) and process access to lsass by Mimikatz are highly observable via EDR process-access and command-line telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttps.procedure_description: The actor runs WebBrowserPassView to extract stored credentials from web browsers on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — WebBrowserPassView execution and its access to browser credential stores (Login Data files) are detectable via known-tool hashes/signatures and file-access telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: On check-in, the Sponsor backdoor collects extensive host information: hostname, BIOS info, processor details, Windows version, domain membership, username, and AC/battery power status.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — the discovery happens inside the backdoor via API calls rather than spawned commands, so it is subtle; detection leans on catching the backdoor process/beacon rather than the enumeration itself

ttps.technique_name: System Location Discovery: System Language Discovery
ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor collects the host timezone and locale/language settings as part of its initial reconnaissance report to the C2.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — locale/timezone queries are in-process and indistinguishable from benign activity; hunt candidate only in the context of the backdoor

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor's 'p' operator command returns a process ID to the operator, providing basic process-context discovery.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — a single PID lookup inside the backdoor is not meaningfully observable on its own; hunt candidate tied to the backdoor

ttps.procedure_description: The actor runs Host2IP (host2ip.exe) to resolve hostnames to IP addresses and map remote systems on the victim network in preparation for lateral movement and tunneling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — execution of host2ip.exe (a non-standard utility) and bursts of name-resolution/host enumeration are detectable via process and DNS telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Following the Host2IP mapping, the actor identifies reachable internal services/hosts to plan pivoting and tunneling deeper into the network.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal service discovery / connection fan-out is detectable via east-west network analytics, though it can blend with legitimate scanning tools

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor communicates with its C2 over HTTP on port 80, polling at a configurable interval defined in config.txt.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — periodic HTTP/80 beacons from a service process to the known Sponsor C2 IPs are detectable via network/proxy telemetry and beacon-interval analytics, especially when correlated with the C2 IOCs

ttps.procedure_description: Sponsor encrypts its C2 message contents with RC4 (a symmetric cipher) before transmission over HTTP.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — RC4-encrypted payloads inside plain HTTP produce high-entropy bodies over port 80 that can be flagged heuristically, but confirmation needs payload inspection

ttps.procedure_description: Sponsor Base64-encodes its (RC4-encrypted) C2 messages before sending them over HTTP.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — Base64-encoded blobs in HTTP request/response bodies to the Sponsor C2 are detectable heuristically, particularly combined with the beacon interval and C2 IOCs

ttps.procedure_description: Sponsor obscures its command-and-control traffic by layering RC4 encryption and Base64 encoding, disguising the true content of operator commands and exfiltrated host data.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — obfuscated C2 is best caught via anomaly on the HTTP/80 channel to the Sponsor C2 IPs rather than content signatures

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor's 'd' and 'u' operator commands download and execute additional files, with 'u' using the URLDownloadToFileW API; dedicated tool-delivery servers were used to stage the open-source toolset.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — the Sponsor service or a URLDownloadToFileW call fetching an executable followed by its execution is detectable via process+network+file-write correlation; outbound to the tool-delivery IOCs (5.255.97.172, 198.144.189.74) adds fidelity

ttps.procedure_description: The actor deploys RevSocks (as CSRSS.EXE) and GOST to establish reverse SOCKS proxies / TCP-UDP relays out of the victim network, and Chisel for HTTP/SSH-tunneled proxying.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — execution of RevSocks/GOST/Chisel (by known hash or renamed CSRSS.EXE outside System32) and their outbound reverse-proxy connections are detectable via process and network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: The actor uses Plink (plink.exe) for SSH tunneling and GOST/Chisel to tunnel TCP/UDP/HTTP traffic, relaying connections to bypass network controls and reach internal systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — plink.exe/gost.exe/chisel.exe execution and their tunneling connections are detectable via process command-line and outbound-connection telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: The actor uses Plink (the PuTTY command-line SSH client) to establish SSH connections/tunnels for pivoting between and accessing compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — plink.exe execution and outbound SSH from unusual internal hosts are detectable via process and network telemetry, though SSH can be legitimate in some environments

ttps.procedure_description: Collected host reconnaissance and command output are returned to the operator over the same Base64+RC4-obfuscated HTTP/80 Sponsor C2 channel.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — outbound data returned over the beacon channel is detectable as part of the C2 flow to the Sponsor IOCs, but distinguishing exfil volume from beaconing requires flow analysis

ttps.procedure_description: The Sponsor backdoor's 's' operator command runs Uninstall.bat to remove the backdoor and its artifacts from disk, cleaning up indicators when the operator ends access.
observed_tooling: Sponsor (modular Windows-service backdoor; versions v1-v5, v5 aka Alumina)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — execution of Uninstall.bat and deletion of the service binary/config files (config.txt, node.txt, error.txt) are detectable via process-creation and file-delete telemetry if captured before cleanup completes

ttps.procedure_description: The actor uses SQLExtractor (sqlextractor.exe) to interact with and extract data from SQL databases on compromised hosts, and collects local host data via the backdoor.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — execution of a non-standard sqlextractor.exe and bulk local database reads are detectable via process and file/DB-access telemetry, though it can resemble legitimate DBA activity

detection_signals: Exploitation and post-exploit activity on internet-facing Microsoft Exchange (CVE-2021-26855): unexpected child processes of w3wp.exe / UMWorkerProcess.exe, file writes to inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client, and IIS/Exchange request-log anomalies
Windows service creation (Event ID 7045 / 4697) named 'SystemNetwork' or 'Update' pointing at an unsigned binary in a non-standard path — the core Sponsor persistence signal

Sponsor on-disk artifacts: config.txt, node.txt, error.txt co-located with the service binary; staging under %WINDIR%\Tasks\, %WINDIR%\INF\MSExchange Delivery DSN\, %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Temp\file\, and %SYSTEMDRIVE%\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\
Batch-file installers (install.bat / Uninstall.bat) run via cmd.exe, and the Sponsor binary launched with the 'install' argument
CSRSS.EXE executing from a path other than %WINDIR%\System32 or with a non-Microsoft signature (RevSocks masquerade)
procdump64.exe against lsass and Mimikatz (mi.exe) process access to lsass.exe; WebBrowserPassView accessing browser Login Data stores
Execution of host2ip.exe, sqlextractor.exe, plink.exe, gost.exe, chisel.exe, or SharpTShipper on servers
Periodic HTTP/80 beacons with Base64/high-entropy (RC4) bodies to the Sponsor C2 IPs 37.120.222.168, 5.255.97.172, 198.144.189.74 (and PowerLess C2 162.55.137.20)
Reverse SOCKS / tunneling connections outbound from internal servers (RevSocks, GOST, Chisel, Plink)
notes: Primary source is ESET Research's 'Sponsor batch-filed whiskers: Ballistic Bobcat's Scan & Strike backdoor' (2023-09-11), a primary vendor report with a real IOC appendix and MITRE mappings; enriched only where ESET states the behavior. Attribution: ESET tracks Ballistic Bobcat as a distinct Iran-aligned cluster that overlaps APT35 / Charming Kitten / Phosphorus / Mint Sandstorm — the overlap is stated honestly and NOT resolved here (adjudication belongs to a separate ACH process). attribution_confidence is 'medium' (Iran-aligned is well supported; the exact boundary between Ballistic Bobcat and the Charming Kitten public cluster is not crisply resolved), consistent with the tasking's medium-high framing on the state alignment. actor.mitre_id intentionally left empty per spec; the public MITRE group id G0058 (Charming Kitten) is cited only in source/aliases for cluster overlap, not as this actor's id. ATT&CK normalization: ESET mapped to ATT&CK v13; every technique_id here was validated against THIS environment's bundled dataset (attack_dump.json, 697 techniques) and all are present. Defense-evasion behaviors use the env tactic slug 'stealth'. Indicator-removal via Uninstall.bat is captured as T1070.004 (present in the dump) rather than the T1685.x/T1686.003 Impair-Defenses family, because file deletion of the backdoor's own artifacts is straightforward File Deletion; noted here per spec's substitution-transparency rule. STRONGEST DETECTION SURFACE (detect candidates, high feasibility): T1190 Exchange CVE-2021-26855 exploitation, T1505.003 Exchange/IIS web-root writes, T1543.003/T1569.002 SystemNetwork/Update service, T1059.003 batch/cmd install chain, T1003.001 ProcDump/Mimikatz, T1555.003 WebBrowserPassView, T1036.005 CSRSS.EXE masquerade, T1071.001/T1105 Sponsor HTTP-80 C2 + downloader, T1090/T1572 RevSocks/GOST/Chisel/Plink tunneling. HUNT-leaning (low feasibility, off-victim/subtle): T1595.002 internet scan-and-exploit, T1587.001/T1588.002 capability development & tool acquisition, T1614.001/T1057 in-backdoor discovery. IOCs are taken from the ESET report/appendix: 14 SHA-1 sample hashes (Sponsor v1-v5 plus the RevSocks/ProcDump/Mimikatz/GOST/Chisel/Plink/WebBrowserPassView/SQLExtractor tools), the four C2/tool-delivery IPs, and CVE-2021-26855. One reported Host2IP SHA-1 was returned malformed (43 hex chars) by the fetch and was deliberately DROPPED rather than included as a bad indicator — pull it directly from the ESET malware-ioc STIX package if the Host2IP hash is required. No malicious C2 domains were enumerated in the source (the operation is IP-based), so domains is empty; no YARA rules were published in the report body, so yara_rules is empty (author none per spec). Victimology: 34 organizations — ~31 Israel, 1 Brazil, 1 UAE — reflecting opportunistic scan-and-exploit rather than deliberate victim selection.
